channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] North Carolina’s three port facilities ran cargo by hand for days after a systems-wide cyberattack
item.description: A cyberattack detected on 4 August triggered a systems-wide IT outage at the North Carolina State Ports Authority, forcing the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port onto manual gate processing. Trucks queued and cargo moves slowed across a network that handles more than 320,000 TEU, over four million tonnes of general cargo and roughly 1,000 vessel calls a year. Normal gate schedules resumed on 6 August with processing still being done manually while systems were restored, and officials described the incident as contained. The US Coast Guard says it is monitoring alongside state officials, and outside forensic experts were engaged. NC Ports has not named an attacker, disclosed the access method or confirmed ransomware or data theft, and no group has claimed it. There is no public evidence that terminal OT was reached. - CyberScoop, The Record, WECT — NC Ports confirmed; USCG monitoring - Attack detected 4 Aug 2026; contained and normal gate schedules resumed 6 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Six agencies warn on Gunra ransomware — edge appliances in, transport among named victims
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-222A, published 10 August by CISA, the FBI, DC3, NSA, the Secret Service and South Korea’s National Police Agency, describes Gunra ransomware. Built on leaked Conti source code and first seen in April 2025, Gunra has grown into a ransomware-as-a-service operation with recruited affiliates. Affiliates gain access through exposed edge infrastructure — VPN gateways, firewall appliances and RDP-reachable systems — then exfiltrate before encrypting under a double-extortion model. Named victim sectors include transport, utilities, manufacturing and government. The Korean National Police Agency’s participation is worth noting for shipping specifically, given how much of the world’s newbuild and ship-management IT sits in Korean and Japanese supply chains. - CISA/FBI/NSA joint advisory AA26-222A - Published 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Uber Freight investigating claimed theft of nearly a million files; operations reported unaffected
item.description: Uber Freight said this week it is investigating unauthorized access to part of its systems and repositories after the extortion group Helix claimed to have stolen close to one million files. The company states its operations have not been disrupted and its systems remain secure and fully operational while the investigation continues; the claim itself is unverified. Helix, recently profiled by Google, has also been linked to a campaign against major Wall Street firms. For terminals and shipping lines the relevance is indirect but real: brokerage and drayage platforms hold booking, chassis and appointment data that maps landside flow, and a leak of that material makes an operator more predictable to whoever reads it. - SecurityWeek weekly roundup — company statement; actor claim unverified - Reported 14 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] AA26-097A update: PLC project files rewritten to strip shutdown and alarm logic
item.description: The 22 July update to joint advisory AA26-097A sets out the tradecraft in unusual detail. Iran-affiliated actors connect to internet-exposed controllers using the vendors’ own engineering software — Rockwell Studio 5000 Logix Designer, Schneider EcoStruxure Control Expert and Siemens TIA Portal — over ports 44818, 2222, 102, 502 and 22, then extract, modify and delete project logic. In one US case investigators found a project file that preserved ladder logic for downstream function while adding logic that overrode safe operating parameters and disabled shutdown and alarm functions. Targeted families include Rockwell CompactLogix and Micro850, Schneider Modicon M340 (BMX P34) and Siemens S7-1200. Those controllers run terminal conveyors, bunkering and ballast-water skids, shore-power interfaces, lock and bridge machinery and reefer plant — usually commissioned by an integrator and rarely re-inventoried. - CISA/FBI/NSA/EPA joint advisory AA26-097A; SecurityWeek - Updated 22 Jul 2026 (originally published 7 Apr 2026) — campaign ongoing

item.title: [Medium] Dragos counts 95 transport and logistics ransomware incidents in Q2, none involving direct ICS manipulation
item.description: Dragos’ Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis, published 11 August, recorded 1,140 incidents at industrial organizations, up 12% from 1,020 in Q1. Transportation and logistics accounted for 95 of them; ICS-adjacent firms including engineering companies and system integrators accounted for 117. North America led with 514 incidents and Europe followed with 316. Dragos observed no case during the quarter in which a ransomware operator directly manipulated an industrial control system, yet operations were still interrupted through IT, ERP and virtualization systems. Read against the NC Ports incident, that is the pattern in miniature: the operational damage in maritime comes from losing the terminal operating system, the planning tools and the appointment platform, not from a compromised crane. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis Q2 2026; Help Net Security - Published 11 Aug 2026 (covering Q2 2026)

item.title: [Critical] CVSS 10 unauthenticated root command injection in Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway (ICSA-26-225-02)
item.description: CISA published 14 ICS advisories on 13 August, headed by CVE-2026-19188 in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway at CVSS 10.0. The device’s ‘Net Check’ feature passes user-supplied input from the cmdPing Socket.io event to the operating system without sanitizing it, letting an unauthenticated remote attacker execute arbitrary OS commands as root without user interaction. Version 3.40.1.12 is affected; CISA names energy, critical manufacturing and water among deployment sectors. Maritime is not named, but these combined HMI/gateway/DTU units are the cheap remote-monitoring boxes that show up on bunkering skids, reefer plant, shore-power cabinets, lock and bridge machinery and remote jetties — installed by a contractor, connected over cellular, and absent from the terminal asset register. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-225-02 - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Cisco Secure Firewall ASA/FTD zero-day added to CISA KEV after denial-of-service exploitation
item.description: CISA added three vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 11 August, including CVE-2026-20349, a heap-inspection flaw in Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance and Firewall Threat Defense that Cisco patched after it was exploited as a zero-day for denial-of-service attacks. The others are a use-after-free in the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock (CVE-2026-68820) and SQL injection in Metabase (CVE-2026-72898). CISA also added Progress LoadMaster CVE-2026-8037 on 7 August. ASA and FTD appliances typically sit between a terminal’s corporate network and its operations network and terminate the VPNs used by crane and TOS vendors; knocking one over does not breach the terminal but it removes remote support and monitoring at the moment you would want both. - CISA KEV catalog additions, 7 and 11 Aug 2026 - Cisco ASA/FTD added to KEV 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] August ICS Patch Tuesday: maximum-severity authentication bypass in Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050
item.description: Siemens published 10 advisories on 11 August, led by a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices (SSA-834709) allowing a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. Siemens also patched a critical code-execution flaw in Siveillance Video Management Servers — widely used for terminal and perimeter CCTV — plus high-severity issues in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, the Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort, and medium-severity fixes in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric addressed NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown; Phoenix Contact covered multiple PLCnext firmware flaws exploitable without authentication. Ruggedcom switches and Siveillance servers are the entries most likely to already be inside a port network. - Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric, Phoenix Contact PSIRT via SecurityWeek - Advisories published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] USCG cyber rule: annual training already due each January, plans and assessments by 16 July 2027
item.description: The Coast Guard’s Cybersecurity in the Marine Transportation System rule, issued 17 January 2025 and effective 16 July 2025, is the first enforceable federal framework requiring US-flagged vessels, Outer Continental Shelf facilities and waterfront facilities to implement cybersecurity measures. Reportable cyber incidents have had to go to the National Response Center since the effective date. Personnel training under 33 CFR 101.650 was required by 12 January 2026 and annually thereafter. The remaining milestone is the big one: by 16 July 2027 owners and operators must designate a Cybersecurity Officer, complete a Cybersecurity Assessment and submit a Cybersecurity Plan for approval. The NC Ports incident is a useful stress test of whether your draft plan describes what your team would actually do. - USCG final rule, Cybersecurity in the Marine Transportation System; Dragos compliance summary - Rule issued 17 Jan 2025, effective 16 Jul 2025 — training due each 12 Jan; full compliance 16 Jul 2027

item.title: [Medium] IACS UR E26 and E27 move from paper to verification as covered newbuilds start delivering
item.description: IACS Unified Requirements E26 (cyber resilience of ships) and E27 (cyber resilience of onboard systems and equipment) have applied to vessels contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024. With those hulls now delivering in numbers, the requirements are being verified on real ships rather than assessed on drawings. E26 treats the vessel as a complete system and requires network segmentation, access control and, notably, no IP exposure from onboard systems to untrusted networks; E27 pushes the same expectations down to individual suppliers and equipment. Operators and equipment makers that cannot evidence compliance risk practical consequences at survey and in port. The awkward cases are integrated bridge, engine automation and cargo systems whose vendors expect remote support over the ship’s VSAT link. - IACS Unified Requirements E26 and E27 - Applicable to vessels contracted on or after 1 Jul 2024 — first-generation vessels now delivering
